title: Chapter 9: High Courts – Structure, Powers and Jurisdiction

blocks.content: Every High Court shall be a court of record and shall have all the powers of such a court including the power to punish for contempt of itself.

rows: Can issue writs only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
Can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights
Applicable throughout the entire territory of India
Restricted to state territorial limits or cause of action origin
A guaranteed Fundamental Right; SC cannot refuse relief
Discretionary remedy; HC may refuse to grant writ relief

items: Writ Jurisdiction Scope: Article 226 (High Court) is discretionary and wider than Article 32 (Supreme Court) because High Courts can issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights.

Removal Process: A High Court judge is removed by an order of the President following a motion passed by a special majority in both Houses of Parliament on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
Qualifications: To be appointed as a High Court judge, a person must be a citizen of India and have held a judicial office in India for 10 years or been an advocate of a High Court for 10 years.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Article 214 provides that there shall be a High Court for each state, while the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1956 authorized Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more states or union territories.
High Court judges are appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the state, and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court.
Under Article 226, High Courts possess writ jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights as well as ordinary legal rights, giving it a wider remedial scope than the Supreme Court under Article 32.
Article 215 designates every High Court as a Court of Record, granting it power to punish for contempt of court and maintaining its judgments as perpetual records.
Article 227 confers administrative and judicial superintendence upon High Courts over all subordinate courts and tribunals within its jurisdiction, excluding military tribunals.
